newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Sweden's Wallenbergs may loosen domestic grip.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sweden's Wallenbergs may loosen domestic grip.

text.p: Sweden's mighty business family, the Wallenbergs, have once again demonstrated their tight grip on Swedish industry in this week's reshuffle of chief executives in three of the country's largest companies.

But with globalisation and tougher competition in the wind, the Wallenbergs might be forced to loosen their hold on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, where they control roughly 40 percent of shares, in favour of foreign growth shares, analysts said.
On Monday, three Wallenberg-sphere executives took the helm of two companies within the "family", appliance maker Electrolux AB and engineering group Atlas Copco AB.
A Wallenberg man, Electrolux boss Leif Johansson, took charge of Volvo, which is firmly outside the Wallenberg empire.
Johansson will in turn will be replaced by Atlas Copco chief executive Michael Treschow, whose job will be filled by Giulio Mazzalupi, a senior executive of the engineering group.
Analysts did not see Johansson's move to Volvo as a Wallenberg attempt to take over a company that was run by rival Pehr Gyllenhammar from 1971 to 1993.
During that time Volvo and the Wallenbergs were involved in a number of cross-ownerships, which helped to curb their rivalry.

"Although you could say that the Wallenbergs are partly advancing their position in Volvo, you should rather see the whole deal as Johansson receiving a job offer," said Mats Larsson, analyst at Swedish bank Swedbank.
CYCLICAL SHARES OUT, FOREIGN GROWTH SHARES IN

As far as the Wallenbergs are concerned, cyclical shares such as automotive stocks are out and foreign growth shares are in, analysts said, referring to statements from the family's key investment vehicle, Investor AB.
"Investor has said it will target growth sectors outside Sweden: telecommunications, health care, media, IT and financial groups," Gunnar Andersson, analyst at Handelsbanken, told Reuters.
While shifting focus, the Wallenbergs could shed such old family jewels as Electrolux and roller bearing maker SKF AB, analysts said.
The dynasty is not so sentimental as to hang on to holdings just because they have been in the family for decades.
When figuring out what the clan is up to, a sign to look for could be stake reduction below control levels, according to David Bartal, the author of a book about the family.
"They always want control," Bartal told Reuters. "When they do not control a company, they probably want out of it."
An example could be car maker Saab Automobile AB, which is jointly held by Investor and U.S. automotive group General Motors, with GM having management responsibility.
But the family might hold on to its 50 percent stake after pouring huge amounts of money into the loss-making, up-market car manufacturer.
"If Saab Automobile's operations start becoming self-supporting and if there is a possibility of retrieving investments made, they could stick around," Andersson said.
PROFIT MOTIVE NOW STRONGER THAN POWER

The Wallenbergs have had a central influence over 20th century Sweden and are known as a long-haul owner of companies, even through adversity. But the demand for profit now overshadows the quest for power, analysts say.

"The general trend is toward more openness, with social ties meaning less and economic results more," said Leif Vindevag, head of research and international relations at the Stockholm Stock Exchange. "The bottom line is what counts."

Investor's chief executive Claes Dahlback -- in an attempt to rid his share of the discount it trades at -- has emphasised that the company is focusing on building value for shareholders rather than taking decisions based on the pursuit of power.
Currently the Wallenberg hold on Swedish industry is stronger than ever, as it has boosted its stakes in family controlled companies, analysts said.
The key to the empire's power is its holding of A shares, which usually have 10 times more voting rights than ordinary B shares.
Companies within its web include the two most dominant players on the Stockholm bourse, pharmaceutical company Astra and telecoms group Ericsson.
Others are Swiss-Swedish engineering group ABB, forestry group Stora and Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS).
Through Investor's stake in Incentive AB, the clan controls another network of companies, notably medical technology company Gambro.
COULD THE FORTRESS CRUMBLE?
But the family fortress could be on the verge of crumbling, according to Nils Lundgren, chief economist at Nordbanken.
"The dynasty is on its way out," Lundgren told Reuters.
"Peter Wallenberg happened to jump in and proved to be much stronger than anyone had thought. He breathed fresh life into the dynasty and the Wallenberg myth.

"But when he retires, the two young Wallenbergs have to compete with others for influence. If they reach top positions in five or 10 years, it will be because they have proved to be very skilled. If they do not, the Wallenberg era is over."
Peter Wallenberg, who was taunted by his father for not being up to family standards, took over when his brother Marc Wallenberg shot himself with a hunting rifle in 1971.

The next two in line to head the empire are cousins Jacob and Marcus, the namesakes of several forefathers, which reflects a family tradition of passing the same few names down through the generations.
Despite Lundgren's views no one seems willing to bet on the downfall of one of Europe's most powerful financial families.
FAMILY'S POLITICAL ROLE
It is hard to estimate how big the clan's current clout is in Sweden's political life. Historically, the family has played a large and controversial political role.

During World War Two, family members helped negotiate trade links with Nazi Germany and one was deeply involved with a group of German officers who tried but failed to kill Hitler, according to Bartal's book "The Empire".

The best-known family member was perhaps Raoul Wallenberg, the legendary Swedish diplomat who went to Hungary and, with little regard for his own safety, saved tens of thousands of Jews from Nazi death camps in 1944.
He was arrested on January 17, 1945, by Soviet soldiers and his fate remains unknown, although press reports have suggested he died in a Soviet prison in 1947.
Although Raoul Wallenberg attracted a lot of media attention, most Wallenbergs keep out of the media spotlight, following the family's motto: "Esse non videri" -- "To be, but not be seen."
